title: IMO may codify alternative net-zero bunker rules in 2027: US FMC
summary: The IMO's proposed Net-Zero Framework, intended to impose mandatory carbon costs from 2028, faces fierce US opposition over estimated annual expenses reaching hundreds of billions. Washington advocates for a "voluntary" market-based compliance system, effectively pushing back binding financial responsibility for the maritime sector's significant emissions. This protracted debate and push for voluntary measures postpones meaningful financial accountability, allowing continued reliance on high-carbon fuels.
content:
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) may start forming consensus around an alternative Net-Zero Framework (NZF) in the coming weeks before hammering out its final text in 2027, US Federal Maritime Commission Chairman Laura DiBella said.

The UN agency is due to hold meetings Nov. 23-Dec. 4 to discuss the framework, after member states last year voted to delay its adoption by a year amid fierce US opposition.

“I hope we’re going to come to some sort of landing spot,” DiBella told Platts on the sidelines of the International Bunker Industry Association’s annual convention in New York City.

“I don’t think anything will be codified this year — maybe 2027, it will be codified. But I think we’ll come to some sort of consensus,” DiBella said.

The comments from the top US maritime regulator came after Japan, Panama, and some other countries proposed several alternatives to the NZF, which, in its current form, would place a mandatory cost on maritime greenhouse gas emissions from 2028 to promote a low-carbon bunker transition.

The US has estimated that the framework would cost the shipping industry $53 billion-$265 billion annually while arguing the incremental expenses would be ultimately passed on to businesses and consumers.

“We have the potential to take remedial action against the flag states that support it, that deliver cargo to the US,” DiBella said, referring to the FMC’s remit. “As the largest consumer of imported goods, we will face the biggest penalties. We don’t need additional inflationary measures on our cargo.”

But Washington would be open to what it believes to be a commercially realistic, technology-neutral NZF with achievable emissions targets, voluntary market-based compliance, and no mandatory carbon bills collected by the IMO, the US has suggested.

“The United States is working toward a consensus on something so that industry can make the necessary investments [in alternative fuels] and move ahead,” DiBella said.

Gas pathway

DiBella has displayed a favorable attitude toward LNG and bio-LNG and previously said in a web post that based on her personal view, the fuels could meet over 60% of global maritime bunker demand by 2050, and that the US is well positioned to supply the fuels as the world’s top LNG exporter, which could draw investments in increasing bio-LNG output with a “well-designed global fuel standard.

“The infrastructure is there to support it globally … I lean very heavy on the infrastructure side and what’s available and what’s realistic,” she told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy.
